newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lagerfeld's Chanel - the ultimate status symbol.
newsitem.headline: Lagerfeld's Chanel - the ultimate status symbol.

text.p: Chanel topped off the ready-to-wear fashion season on Monday with a collection by Karl Lagerfeld that dripped with status symbols and trendy logos for the house's jet-set clientele.

There were initialled running shoes for those early morning jogs along the beach, insignia bikinis to show off wash-board bellies on Saint Tropez beaches and shimmering slip-dresses for Riviera nightclubs.

Buyers were delighted with Lagerfeld's fitted jackets over riding britches and starched white shirts, his shorts with matching fluid jackets in aqua, mint, lilac or red and stretchy signature tweed evening dresses.

"It was incredible. Karl is so inventive and full of ideas," Rosemarie Bravo, president of Saks Fifth Avenue department stores. "I loved the jodphur pants, the shorts, the evening wear and just the exuberance. It was wonderful from beginning to end."
Claudia Schiffer, the supermodel who used to be Lagerfeld's muse, made her only appearance of the eight-day week of shows on Chanel's catwalk.
Her return was a surprise, following their much publicised falling out last month when Lagerfeld told a French press agency last month: "She should change jobs."
At the time, Schiffer's agent said the supermodel had decided to stop appearing in catwalk shows.
In one of the finest moments of the eight-day fashion season, John Galliano produced a breathtaking farewell collection for the house of Givenchy on Sunday night.

Free of theatrical tricks and costume ball dresses, it cemented his reputation as a brilliant craftsman and fervently imaginative designer as he prepares to take the helm at the more prestigious fashion house of Christian Dior.

LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton, the luxury goods firm that owns both houses, formally named Galliano to take over at Christian Dior on Monday and appointed Britain's Alexander McQueen as his successor.

Galliano's collection was a masterpiece: djellaba braid swirls across a black Victorian jacket, high-waisted gowns with tiny puffed sleeves of silk patterned like Wedgewood china, and the romance of a primrose-strewn blouse, its ruffles tumbling down the shoulders of a diminutive Kate Moss.

It was fantasy that translates into real-life: satin bellhop suits with red ribbon trim, curvy 1940s-style dress in tiny polka dotted fabrics and wing-sleeved jacket of absinthe brocade on a leopard chiffon gown.
During his short tenure at Givenchy, Galliano has transformed the house's strait-laced image into one of romance and drama, propelling the label back to fashion's sharp edge.
The sceptiocs who predicted that Galliano's wild ways and fragile artistic temperment would not hold up under the high-pressure demands of a major label have had to eat their words.
